The Estate · Pinehurst, NC

Some houses hold history. This one shaped it.

The gates have opened onto the same circular drive since 1916. The house at the end of it has not moved.

Build the farm—therefore—and let me hear at every stage of that happy game.   I think of Garran Hill every day. It is the only place I want to be.
Walter Hines Page · 1855–1918

Appointed by Wilson. He held the alliance from London.

Born in Cary, North Carolina. Co-founder of Doubleday, Page & Company. Editor of The Atlantic Monthly. Appointed by Woodrow Wilson as Ambassador to the Court of St. James in 1913 — and kept there through the years the world came apart.

From London, he commissioned Garran Hill to be built on his family’s Moore County acres. He named it himself. Page returned from London in December 1918. He did not return to Garran Hill.

“Well, Frank, I did get here after all, didn't I?” — Aberdeen station, December 1918.

“Build the farm, therefore; and let me hear at every stage of that happy game.”

Walter Hines Page — Letter, 1918

“The farm — the farm — the farm.”

Walter Hines Page · From His Letters · 1913–1918

“The farm — the farm — the farm.”

Built in Brick

Pinehurst hands. A century of brick and proportion.

Garran Hill's authority begins in its masonry: full-brick Neo-Georgian construction, red handmade brick laid in Flemish bond, and a traditional water table grounding the facade. The brickwork, the arched fanlights, the entry floor — all built by hand in Moore County between 1915 and 1916. During restoration, matching the original brick alone took three months. That is the standard to which every decision was held.

Boston plans. Pinehurst hands. Garran Hill in brick, 1916.

The Threshold · 1916

The door has been open since 1916.

Before the house opens, it speaks. The estate’s original name is cut into the stone underfoot: Garran Hill, 1916. The brick reads it before you cross the threshold.

Everything you are about to see was here before you arrived. The brass key plates on every door still have their original keys.

Restoration
The Restoration · 1999–2001

What was original stayed original.

The restoration did not make Garran Hill new. It made it whole again. Original elements remain where they matter most: carved fireplace mantels, oak flooring, leaded-glass sidelights, the arched fanlight at the entry, solid-wood interior doors, brass key plates, and the dining room frontispiece. New systems were woven behind old grace. Not renovated into anonymity. Restored back into itself.

Matching the old brick on the portico alone took three months. That is the standard to which every decision in this restoration was held.

Fifteen pages of drawings — elevations, floor plans, foundation, framing, portico, kitchen, primary suite, library built-ins, trim profiles. Every decision documented before a board came down. The drawings transfer with the property.

The Foyer · 1916

The arched fanlights. The herringbone brick underfoot.

The mahogany volute staircase rises to the right. The leaded glass is original. The brick pattern beneath your feet was laid in 1916. This is the first thing the house shows you — and it doesn’t apologize for any of it.

The Salon

The house's great living room.

Nearly forty feet from end to end. The red walls pull everything inward and warm. The eye goes to the white Georgian fireplace first — carved mantel, art arranged above it with intention. Then to the far end, where glass doors open to the brick terrace. Two seating areas. Arched fanlights. The Salon is the room where everyone eventually lands.

The Drawing Room

Tiled fireplace. Intimate scale. A spiral stair to the office above.

The fire is lit in the frame and the whole room shifts register — from formal to private. Blue walls, white woodwork, Delft-tiled fireplace surround. The Drawing Room is smaller than the Salon by design: it was always meant to be the room you retreat to. The bookshelves flank it. The flame holds the center.

"Blue-and-white tile, firelight, and a spiral stair — the Drawing Room keeps its own rhythm."

The Dining Room

The table has been set in this room since 1916.

The dining table anchors the room — long, dark, centered under the chandelier. The shell cabinets flanking the fireplace are original to the house. The wallpaper is a print that has been here since the restoration and reads like the room always knew what it wanted to be. The folding screen that divides the room from the hall folds and disappears. It has been doing that since 1916.

Kitchen & Butler’s Pantry · The Restoration

White cabinetry. Dark granite. Island.
Four windows. Room to cook.

The kitchen was not updated. It was designed.

The Origin

The kitchen is not original to 1916.
It is original to the restoration.

The original kitchen was in the basement. When the stewards rebuilt Garran Hill from 1999 to 2001, they designed the kitchen from scratch — not as an update, but as an act of architectural discipline. Heart-pine floors, not the oak of the original rooms. A distinction that tells you exactly what this space is and when it arrived.

The Details

The island doubles as a dinette. Matte black granite counters. Two farm sinks — one anchoring the kitchen, one in the open butler’s pantry. A wall of windows over the main sink faces grass, magnolias, American plane trees, and the pool beyond.

Sub-Zero refrigerator. Custom cabinetry. A black-and-white toile wallpaper that carries the history of the house without announcing it. The grounds are visible through every window.

The Proof

The restoration was not guessed into place. It was drawn, measured, and built.

Sheet 12 of the restoration drawings documents the kitchen cabinetry in elevation — cooking wall, cornice, pantry, desk, and TV cabinet, all drawn before they were built. The architectural plans, all 15 sheets, transfer with the property.

The Extension

The kitchen does not stop at the wall. The adjoining side porch carries hot and cold water, built-in cabinets and shelves, and a full potting bench — the working infrastructure of an estate that takes its grounds seriously.

The Library · 1916

The books have been here longer than anyone alive.

The shelving on three walls holds what was left behind and what was brought in. The rolling ladder runs the full width. The French doors open to the grounds. In the afternoon, the light through those doors crosses the floor and reaches the spines on the opposite wall. This is the room the house was built around.

When you stand in it, you cannot find the seam.

The Primary Suite

A fireplace. Two windows. The grounds on both sides.

The fireplace is centered, flanked by two upholstered armchairs. Soft natural light from the windows to the left. The palette is pastel — yellows, greens, a touch of blue — quiet colors for a room designed to be a place of actual rest. The primary suite occupies the corner of the second floor and opens to a private balcony overlooking the rear grounds and tennis courts. Mornings here face the trees.

The Staircase · 1916

The same curve since 1916.

The mahogany volute turns from the foyer in a single continuous arc — black railing, wooden treads, the wallpaper rising beside it. It has not been replaced. It has not been rebuilt. It has been climbed every day, by every person who has lived in this house, since the craftsmen Leonard Tufts sent finished it in 1916. The curve is the original curve.

The stair still gives the entry its first gesture of grace.

Private Rooms

The Second Floor.

The primary suite has a fireplace and custom wall paneling. Four bedrooms total — each shaped during restoration for proportion and light.

Primary bath, primary closet, and upper hall all documented in the restoration drawings. The private floor was treated with the same architectural discipline as the social rooms below.

The Primary Bath

Mirror. Marble. Ornament that earns its place.

The primary bath reads like a jewel box — the wallpaper is floral and dense, the sink is centered and ornate, the Tennessee marble is warm underfoot, the light is warm and deliberate. Everything in this room was chosen to contrast with the scale of the house around it. It is small on purpose. The detail is the point.

The Powder Room

Fuchsia chinoiserie. A room that does not apologize.

The fuchsia wallpaper is the whole point. Chinoiserie pattern, floor to ceiling, Tennessee marble beneath it. This is the most opinionated room in the house — designed to stop you, make you look, make you feel something. The brass key plate on the door still holds its original key. It works. It has always worked.

The House Keeps Secrets

Garran Hill rewards the close observer.

The curved banister. The original hardware. The way the light moves through the leaded glass at different hours. This house was built by craftsmen who cared about things no one would ever notice — and then noticed them anyway. The secrets are still here. They reveal themselves slowly.

The house still knows how to keep a secret.

A Private History · 1959–1984

Horses. Hounds. Peacocks. Native hollies on every path.

Betty Dumaine kept this land for twenty-five years. Left to Duke University after her death. Advertised in Atlanta and New York. No buyer came. The house waited. She brought horses to the grounds of Garran Hill — thoroughbreds, hunters, a life organized around animals and land and the particular pleasure of a place that required real attention. She renamed the property Hollycrest — for the large native hollies at the front of the house. They are still there. One horse she buried here. Blue Fox. The stone is still standing in the shade of the trees she planted. The iron post beside the drive still carries the ring. Someone still puts flowers at the grave.

Betty Dumaine’s Hollycrest years carried horses, hounds, peacocks, native hollies, and old Pinehurst lore to the estate. Her Irish hunter, Blue Fox, is buried on the grounds. Someone still puts flowers there. There was once a four-foot statue of a blue fox beside the grave. It disappeared after she died.

Someone still puts flowers there.

The Grounds
The Terrace · Open Air

The world outside these gates does not exist here.

The terrace opens off the Salon through glass doors. Brick underfoot — the same material as the house, the same that engraves 1916 at the threshold. The lattice railing is white. The loungers face outward toward the treeline. On a clear afternoon the sky above the canopy is an uninterrupted blue. This is where the house ends and the land begins.

Brick underfoot. French doors behind. Garden beyond.

The Side Porch

Where the house meets the garden.

On the side of the house, a porch built for the work of living here. A sink with hot and cold water. Cabinets and shelves. A potting bench where the outdoors comes in. This is the kind of detail that tells you how someone thought about what a house is for.

The irrigation system runs to 28 zones, fed by a 130-foot well. The plantings are not decorative. They are tended.

The Courts · Grounds

Two regulation courts.
Professional lighting.
Night play.

Most estates at this price have one court. Garran Hill has two — full regulation size, commercial fencing, professional lighting installed for night play. The infrastructure is serious. The surfaces await renewal — a straightforward investment that restores the courts to full use.

The Pool · Salt Water

Twenty by forty feet. The gate opens onto it directly.

Through old iron gates, the 20×40 in-ground concrete pool catches afternoon light inside its brick walls. Converted from chlorine to saltwater in 2022, it belongs to the landscape rather than interrupting it.

The Wee Cottage

A cottage in the azaleas. Its own complete world.

Built as a children's playhouse — its own architecture, its own scale, its own silence. Now tucked into the grounds behind a wall of azaleas and tall trees, the Wee Cottage has its own entrance, its own scale, its own quality of light. Guest quarters. Studio. The possibility of a life lived slightly apart from the main house, on the same four-point-fifteen acres.

A small house within the larger story.

4.15 Acres · Moore County

From above, the estate explains itself.

Garran Hill sits within its own 4.15-acre circle — the surviving house core of a much larger Page-era farm.

Inside the gates: circular drive, lawn, brick terrace, pool, gardens, and shade.
